Thank you for the introduction. I found Q3.4 quite challenging because tracking online activity feels invasive, but it might help identify struggling students early. The most important questions for me are about fairness—ensuring all student groups are equally supported.

I was surprised to see that many would never use race/ethnicity data even if it improved fairness. As an international student, I believe such data could help address disparities. Maybe someone else sees value in using it carefully? An opt-out mechanism might balance concerns about privacy and the need for targeted support.

Thank you for starting this discussion.

I found Q3.5 particularly challenging because some sensitive data types, like financial aid status, could significantly improve identification but raise ethical concerns. The most important questions for me are about explainability—understanding why a student is flagged is crucial for providing appropriate support and building trust.

I was surprised by the strong opposition to using nationality data even if it improves fairness. As an advisor, I see how different nationalities might face unique challenges. Perhaps we could explore anonymized or aggregated data use to address privacy concerns while still improving fairness.

Additionally, I think an opt-out mechanism could help balance invasive tracking like online activity with early identification needs.

Thank you for this opportunity to share my thoughts.

As someone who has used disability support services, I believe that targeted support can make a significant difference. I also think an opt-out mechanism could help balance invasive tracking with early identification needs.

For me, the most important questions are about fairness and privacy. I was surprised by the strong opposition to using first-generation student status data; as someone who switched programs, targeted support could have made a difference for me.
